claim: Immediate early genes (IEGs), such as Fos or Arc, rapidly transcribe and express following recent neuronal activity.
source: Immediate early genes (IEGs), such as Fos or Arc, are a class of genes that rapidly transcribe and express following recent neuronal activity (Hunt et al., 1987; Lyford et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunt et al., 1987 and Lyford et al., 1995

claim: Peak IEG responses range from the scale of minutes for RNA expression to minutes and hours for protein expression.
source: Peak IEG responses range from the scale of minutes for RNA expression to minutes and hours for protein expression (Guzowski et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guzowski et al., 2005

claim: IEG expression has been used as a proxy for neural activity.
source: Because of its time-dependent nature, IEG expression has often been used as a proxy for neural activity.
evidence: Based on established scientific practice and knowledge

claim: High-throughput mapping of IEGs has been useful in relating complex behaviors in rodents to their underlying brain activation patterns.
source: As such, high-throughput mapping of IEGs has been immensely useful in relating complex behaviors in rodents to their underlying brain activation (i.e., ensemble) patterns.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and practice

claim: Intact tissue clearing methods have been developed for brain-wide activity mapping.
source: The advent of effective intact tissue clearing methods (Chung et al., 2013; Renier et al., 2014; Susaki et al., 2015; Ueda et al., 2020), microscopy advances (Ragan et al., 2012; Reynaud et al., 2015), and automated registration and cell segmentation pipelines (Renier et al., 2016) has made brain-wide activity mapping projects both scalable and feasible.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published methods

claim: Brain-wide activity mapping has been applied to study brain activation after psilocybin, ketamine, and haloperidol administration.
source: Recent studies have applied these methods to study brain activation during a wide variety of experiences, including after psilocybin, ketamine, and haloperidol administration (Davoudian et al., 2023; Renier et al., 2016), the incubation of palatable food craving (Madangopal et al., 2022), and fear memory (Franceschini et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies

claim: Almost all brain-wide activity mapping approaches have focused on mapping single ensembles across the brain.
source: However, with a few exceptions, almost all of these approaches have focused on mapping single ensembles across the brains.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Activity-dependent tagging approaches allow for the investigation of multiple ensembles and their shared overlap during two distinct experiences within the same subjects.
source: Over the last decade, activity-dependent tagging approaches, such as the tamoxifen-inducible ArcCreERT2 (Denny et al., 2014) and TRAP1/TRAP2 systems (DeNardo et al., 2019; Guenthner et al., 2013), or the doxycycline-controlled TetTag system (Reijmers et al., 2007), have allowed for the investigation of multiple ensembles—and their shared overlap—during two distinct experiences within the same subjects.
evidence: Supported by citations to published tagging systems

claim: Activity-dependent tagging methods have generated unprecedented insight into the neural mechanisms of memory formation, storage, and retrieval.
source: Such tagging methods have generated unprecedented insight into the neural mechanisms of memory formation, storage, and retrieval by allowing for the identification of individual memory traces.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the field

claim: A memory trace or 'engram' refers to the enduring physical substrate of memory and is defined as a neural population initially active during memory encoding whose reactivation at a later time point results in memory retrieval.
source: A memory trace or 'engram' (Semon, 1921) refers to the enduring physical substrate of memory and is defined as a neural population initially active during memory encoding whose reactivation at a later time point results in memory retrieval.
evidence: Supported by citation to Semon, 1921 and established definition in the field

claim: The majority of engram studies have focused on a few focal regions rather than numerous regions across the brain.
source: However, the majority of engram studies have focused on a few focal regions, such as the dentate gyrus (DG; Denny et al., 2014), retrosplenial area (RSP; Cowansage et al., 2014), medial prefrontal cortex (Kitamura et al., 2017), and amygdalar subdivisions, such as the lateral amygdalar nucleus (LA), and basolateral amygdalar nucleus (BLA; Reijmers et al., 2007), rather than the investigation of numerous regions across the brain.
evidence: Supported by citations to specific studies and review of literature

claim: High-throughput mapping and analysis of multiple ensembles poses many challenges including immunolabeling, segmentation, identification of overlapping populations, atlas registration, data management, and analytical methods.
source: In part, this is because high-throughput mapping and analysis of multiple ensembles poses many challenges: (1) Both activity markers need to be clearly immunolabeled across all brain structures under investigation; (2) both labeled markers need to be accurately segmented or automatically counted; (3) a validated strategy needs to be employed for identification of overlapping cell populations; (4) all cell counts and co-labeled cells need to be accurately registered to a standardized atlas space; (5) an infrastructure facilitating easy data management, aggregation, and transformation (e.g., normalizing cell counts by volume) needs to exist; and (6) analytical and visualization methods to intuit functional connectivity between brain regions and how they differ between experimental groupings should be easily implemented.
evidence: Based on logical analysis of technical requirements

claim: The authors developed a workflow incorporating features to make large-scale analysis of traditionally coronally sectioned datasets produced by activity-dependent tagging systems more accessible.
source: Here, we developed a workflow incorporating these features to make large-scale analysis of traditionally coronally sectioned datasets produced by activity-dependent tagging systems more accessible.
evidence: Direct statement of the authors' work

claim: SMARTTR is a versatile R package that wraps mapping capabilities to the common coordinate framework (CCF) of the Allen Brain Institute with functions for statistical analysis and network visualization for multiple ensembles using graph theory.
source: Intrinsic to this pipeline is SMARTTR, a versatile R package that wraps mapping capabilities to the common coordinate framework (CCF) of the Allen Brain Institute (Wang et al., 2020) with functions for statistical analysis and network visualization for multiple ensembles using graph theory.
evidence: Direct description of the SMARTTR package with citation to Allen Brain Institute framework

claim: The SMARTTR package can be applied to imported mapped datasets from other alternative imaging, segmentation, and registration workflows.
source: Moreover, this package is versatile, such that the analysis modules can be easily applied to imported mapped datasets from other alternative imaging, segmentation, and registration workflows, including those reliant on alternative atlas ontologies, such as the Unified Anatomical Atlas (Chon et al., 2019).
evidence: Direct statement of package capabilities with citation to alternative atlas

claim: The pipeline has been designed and validated with the ArcCreERT2 tagging system.
source: While we have designed and validated this pipeline with the ArcCreERT2 tagging system (Denny et al., 2014), the steps and analysis software used in this pipeline are generalizable to virtually all widely used dual-ensemble tagging systems.
evidence: Direct statement of validation with citation

claim: The steps and analysis software used in this pipeline are generalizable to virtually all widely used dual-ensemble tagging systems.
source: While we have designed and validated this pipeline with the ArcCreERT2 tagging system (Denny et al., 2014), the steps and analysis software used in this pipeline are generalizable to virtually all widely used dual-ensemble tagging systems.
evidence: Based on design principles and inference from validation

claim: The pipeline has broader use in allowing for the comparison of brain-wide activity patterns during any two distinct experiences.
source: Beyond its direct application to engram research, this pipeline has broader use in allowing for the comparison of brain-wide activity patterns during any two distinct experiences.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the pipeline's capabilities

claim: The authors applied the workflow to gain novel insight into brain-wide functional activation patterns underlying the acquisition and expression of learned helplessness (LH).
source: To demonstrate the versatility of our workflow, we applied this approach to gain novel insight into brain-wide functional activation patterns underlying the acquisition and expression of learned helplessness (LH), a robust behavioral paradigm which models traumatic stress.
evidence: Direct statement of the application with experimental data

claim: Learned helplessness is a robust behavioral paradigm which models traumatic stress.
source: To demonstrate the versatility of our workflow, we applied this approach to gain novel insight into brain-wide functional activation patterns underlying the acquisition and expression of learned helplessness (LH), a robust behavioral paradigm which models traumatic stress.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field

claim: Wide-scale mapping of ensembles underlying both acquisition and expression of LH has not been studied in the context of LH.
source: To our knowledge, wide-scale mapping of ensembles underlying both of these time points has not been studied in the context of LH and would allow for greater functional insight into changes occurring between these stages.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: The authors identified several altered functional connectivity signatures of the ensembles active during exposure to IS, ES, as well as the shared ensemble population between these experiences.
source: In this effort, we have identified several altered functional connectivity signatures of the ensembles active during exposure to IS, escapable shock (ES), as well as the shared ensemble population between these experiences.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from experimental data

claim: The work is presented as a reference dataset freely available for download and walkthrough alongside an accompanying tutorial.
source: Finally, we have presented this work as a reference dataset freely available for download and walkthrough alongside an accompanying tutorial.
evidence: Direct statement of data availability

claim: The ArcCreERT2 mouse line leverages the activity-dependent expression of the IEG Arc to enable permanent fluorescent tagging of neural ensembles with enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (eYFP).
source: The ArcCreERT2 mouse line leverages the activity-dependent expression of the IEG Arc to enable permanent fluorescent tagging of neural ensembles with enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (eYFP) (Figure 1A; Denny et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Denny et al., 2014 and Figure 1A

claim: Injection of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) opens a transient window for labeling recently active neurons with eYFP in the ArcCreERT2 system.
source: In this system, injection of a selective estrogen receptor agonist, such as 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT), opens a transient window for labeling recently active neurons with eYFP.
evidence: Based on established mechanism of the ArcCreERT2 system

claim: Staining for IEG protein expression (i.e., c-Fos) at a second time point allows for the identification of active ensembles driven by two different behavioral experiences.
source: Staining for IEG protein expression (i.e., c-Fos) at a second time point allows for the identification of active ensembles driven by two different behavioral experiences (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on the dual-labeling strategy and Figure 1B

claim: The pipeline workflow is organized into three different components: immunolabeling and imaging acquisition, image preprocessing and automatic segmentation, and atlas registration and downstream analyses.
source: Following tissue perfusion and brain extraction, multiple ensemble mapping through the pipeline workflow was organized into three different components: (1) immunolabeling and imaging acquisition, (2) image preprocessing and automatic segmentation of dual ensembles and their overlap in ImageJ/FIJI, and (3) atlas registration and downstream analyses in our software package in R (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct description of the workflow with reference to Figure 1C

claim: The authors employed an optimized approach for staining Arc-expressing eYFP+ cells and c-Fos+ cells in thick serial coronal sections based on previous work.
source: For the immunolabeling and imaging acquisition, we employed an optimized approach for staining Arc-expressing eYFP+ cells and c-Fos+ cells in thick serial coronal sections based on our previous work (Leal Santos et al., 2021; Pavlova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: A traditional serial sectioning approach was used because it is the most accessible and reliable way to stain two markers at a high signal-to-noise ratio across deep brain structures.
source: A traditional serial sectioning approach was used, as it is the most accessible and reliable way to stain two markers at a high signal-to-noise ratio across deep brain structures.
evidence: Based on technical reasoning and established practice

claim: A custom segmentation strategy in ImageJ/FIJI uses open-source image processing plugins for accurate cell segmentation in 3D based on the staining morphology characteristics of eYFP+ and c-Fos+ cells.
source: Following imaging for eYFP+ (channel 1) and c-Fos+ (channel 2) cells using a scanning confocal microscope (Leica TCS SP8, Leica Microsystems Inc, Wetzlar, Germany) (Figure 1D), we implemented a custom segmentation strategy in ImageJ/FIJI which uses a suite of open-source image processing plugins (Ollion et al., 2013) for accurate cell segmentation in 3D based on the staining morphology characteristics of eYFP+ and c-Fos+ cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct description of the method with citation and reference to figures

claim: Co-labeled (eYFP+/c-Fos+) cells were identified by comparing all possible overlapping objects using the 3D MultiColoc plugin.
source: Next, co-labeled (eYFP+/c-Fos+) cells were identified by comparing all possible overlapping objects using the open-source 3D MultiColoc plugin (Ollion et al., 2013), saving the output as .txt files, and thresholding by percent volume overlap downstream.
evidence: Direct description of the method with citation

claim: The segmentation and colocalization algorithms were efficiently applied in-batch using custom-written ImageJ/FIJI macros that are freely available for download.
source: The segmentation and colocalization algorithms were efficiently applied in-batch using custom-written ImageJ/FIJI macros that are freely available for download (Source code 3, Source code 4, Source code 5).
evidence: Direct statement of method and data availability

claim: The macros have been generalized to allow for easy parameter modification through a graphical user interface (GUI) to account for different imaging resolutions and unique naming conventions.
source: Importantly, these macros have been generalized to allow for easy parameter modification through a graphical user interface (GUI), to account for different imaging resolutions and unique naming conventions.
evidence: Direct description of the software features

claim: Raw images were collapsed across all z-planes and channels to use as an aggregate reference image for registration to atlas templates from the Allen Institute Mouse Brain Atlas.
source: In the final preprocessing step, since registration is performed on single-plane .tiff images, we collapsed raw images across all z-planes and channels to use as an aggregate reference image for registration to atlas templates from the Allen Institute Mouse Brain Atlas (Lein et al., 2007; Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct description of the method with citations

claim: The SMARTTR package includes a high-level application programming interface (API) which facilitates interactive user-friendly registration, mapping of cell counts, and easy statistical analysis and visualization of multiple ensemble datasets.
source: The SMARTTR package (simple multi-ensemble atlas registration and statistical testing in R) includes a high-level application programming interface (API) which facilitates interactive user-friendly registration, mapping of cell counts, and easy statistical analysis and visualization of multiple ensemble datasets (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct description of the package features with reference to Figure 1F

claim: The standard API was designed around an object-oriented infrastructure where data is managed using slice, mouse, and experiment objects which store additional metadata in a hierarchical manner.
source: This standard API was designed around an object-oriented infrastructure. In the package, data is managed using slice, mouse, and experiment objects which also store additional metadata in a hierarchical manner.
evidence: Direct description of the software architecture

claim: A slice object contains all imaging-related metadata such as the image ID, image path, channel names, and a matching anterior–posterior atlas coordinate, alongside registration data and imported segmentation data.
source: For example, a slice object contains all imaging-related metadata such as the image ID, image path, channel names, and a matching anterior–posterior atlas coordinate, alongside registration data and imported segmentation data.
evidence: Direct description of the data structure

claim: Slice objects are hierarchically stored inside mouse objects, which contain additional metadata such as mouse ID, sex, strain, and genotype.
source: Slice objects are hierarchically stored inside mouse objects, which contain additional metadata such as mouse ID, sex, strain, and genotype.
evidence: Direct description of the data structure

claim: Package functions for interactive registration, importation of segmentation outputs, mapping cell counts to a standard atlas space, automated network analysis, and visualization operate directly on these objects.
source: Package functions for interactive registration, importation of segmentation outputs, mapping cell counts to a standard atlas space, automated network analysis, and visualization operate directly on these objects.
evidence: Direct description of the software functionality

claim: The SMARTTR package includes additional capabilities such as data quality checking for outlier counts, removal of regions to omit due to tissue damage, and normalizing co-labeled counts by a particular channel.
source: Moreover, there are also a suite of additional capabilities, including data quality checking for outlier counts, removal of regions to omit due to tissue damage, and normalizing co-labeled counts by a particular channel.
evidence: Direct description of the software features

claim: The organization of the SMARTTR package facilitates alternative pipeline entry points.
source: The organization of the SMARTTR package also facilitates alternative pipeline entry points.
evidence: Direct statement of the software design

claim: Import functions exist for alternate segmentation approaches.
source: Import functions exist for alternate segmentation approaches.
evidence: Direct statement of the software capabilities

claim: Compatibility with datasets previously registered and mapped with alternative workflows is supported.
source: Compatibility with datasets previously registered and mapped with alternative workflows (Eastwood et al., 2019; Jin et al., 2022; Renier et al., 2016; Yates et al., 2019) is supported (Figure 1F), allowing users to take advantage of the analysis and visualization capabilities of this package without reliance on prior processing steps.
evidence: Direct statement with citations to alternative workflows

claim: Extensive documentation of the package functions and a detailed tutorial using the datasets from this study are available at the package website.
source: Extensive documentation of the package functions and a detailed tutorial using the datasets from this study are available at the package website (https://mjin1812.github.io/SMARTTR/).
evidence: Direct statement of documentation availability

claim: ArcCreERT2 mice were injected with 4-OHT 5 hr prior to exposure to a series of inescapable footshocks on one side of a shuttle box to label active ensembles with eYFP during LH acquisition.
source: To label active ensembles with eYFP during LH acquisition, we injected ArcCreERT2 mice with 4-OHT 5 hr prior to exposure to a series of inescapable footshocks on one side of a shuttle box (IS, inescapable shock group) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Direct description of the experimental procedure with reference to Figure 2A

claim: A second group of ArcCreERT2 mice underwent an identical procedure without experiencing footshocks (CT, context trained group).
source: A second group of ArcCreERT2 mice underwent an identical procedure without experiencing footshocks (CT, context trained group).
evidence: Direct description of the experimental procedure

claim: Following 3 days of dark housing, mice underwent 30 trials in which they could escape footshocks by crossing to the opposite chamber of the shuttle box.
source: Following 3 days of dark housing, mice underwent 30 trials in which they could escape footshocks by crossing to the opposite chamber of the shuttle box.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental procedure

claim: Ninety minutes following the start of testing, mice were sacrificed, and brains were extracted for investigation of c-Fos expression.
source: Ninety minutes following the start of testing, mice were sacrificed, and brains were extracted for investigation of c-Fos expression.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental procedure

claim: Average habituation activity (IR beam breaks) decreases in the shock group.
source: During a 3-min habituation period prior to IS testing, locomotor activity was significantly decreased in the IS group (Figure 2B), indicating a fearful association was established with the shuttle box chamber.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Prior administration of inescapable shocks increases subsequent escape latency across 30 trials of shocks.
source: Across all trials during testing, escape latency was consistently higher in the IS group compared to the CT group (Figure 2C), and average latency to cross for trials 11–30 of the testing phase was significantly greater for the IS group compared to the CT group (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D

claim: A custom algorithm was applied to limit segmentation of cellular processes for eYFP staining.
source: To account for the dendritic/axonal staining pattern of eYFP, a custom algorithm was applied to limit segmentation of cellular processes (Figure 2I; Source code 4).
evidence: Direct description of the method with reference to Figure 2I and source code

claim: The eYFP staining pattern is characteristic of other tagging approaches, for example, TRAP1/TRAP2, making the algorithm likely generalizable to other activity-dependent tagging mechanisms.
source: Since this staining pattern is characteristic of other tagging approaches, for example, TRAP1/TRAP2 (DeNardo et al., 2019; Guenthner et al., 2013), this algorithm is likely generalizable to other activity-dependent tagging mechanisms.
evidence: Based on inference from similarity to other methods with citations

claim: c-Fos localizes to the cell body, resulting in a punctate filled-spherical staining.
source: Since c-Fos localizes to the cell body, resulting in a punctate filled-spherical staining, a separate optimized algorithm for segmenting this expression pattern was applied (Figure 2J; Source code 3).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of c-Fos staining characteristics

claim: All possible segmented object overlaps were compared, and the proportion of volumetric overlap was calculated relative to the volume of segmented c-Fos+ cells.
source: Next, all possible segmented object overlaps were compared, and the proportion of volumetric overlap was calculated (relative to the volume of segmented c-Fos+ cells).
evidence: Direct description of the method

claim: Colocalized cell counts were identified by thresholding by proportion of volume overlap downstream using SMARTTR.
source: Colocalized cell counts were identified by thresholding by proportion of volume overlap downstream using SMARTTR (Figure 2K).
evidence: Direct description of the method with reference to Figure 2K

claim: Automated segmentation results for eYFP+ cells were highly correlated with manual cell counts across both annotators (r = 0.85 averaged manual counts).
source: For eYFP+, we found that automated segmentation results were highly correlated with manual cell counts across both annotators (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–H; r = 0.85 averaged manual counts), and there was high correlation between independent manual counts (r = 0.92).
evidence: Supported by validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: For eYFP+ segmentation, average precision was 0.92, average recall was 0.76, and the averaged overall F1 score was 0.85.
source: We found that average precision (P = TP/(TP + FP)) was 0.92 and average recall (R = TP/(TP + FN)) was 0.76. The averaged overall F1 score, calculated as the harmonic mean of precision and recall (1/F1 = (1/P + 1/R)/2), was 0.85.
evidence: Supported by validation data

claim: For c-Fos+ cells, automated cell counts were highly correlated with manual cell counts across both annotators (r = 0.93 averaged manual counts).
source: For c-Fos+ cells, we similarly found high correlation between automated cell counts and manual cell counts across both annotators (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J–Q; r = 0.93 averaged manual counts), as well as high correlation between annotators (r = 0.93).
evidence: Supported by validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The c-Fos-optimized algorithm yielded an average precision of 0.96, an average recall of 0.78, and an average F1 score of 0.86.
source: The c-Fos-optimized algorithm yielded an average precision of 0.96, an average recall of 0.78, and an average F1 score of 0.86.
evidence: Supported by validation data

claim: Both algorithms faithfully reflected results that would be obtained from typical manual cell counting approaches and even outperformed metrics reported previously for other automatic segmentation approaches for activity-dependent labeled cells.
source: Overall, these results indicate that both algorithms faithfully reflected results that would be obtained from typical manual cell counting approaches and even outperformed metrics reported previously for other automatic segmentation approaches for activity-dependent labeled cells (Franceschini et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on comparison of validation metrics with citation to previous work

claim: During LH acquisition, global brain-wide neural activation levels did not differ between groups.
source: Interestingly, during LH acquisition, global brain-wide neural activation levels did not differ between groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: There were no differences in overall activity among all targeted brain regions between groups during LH acquisition.
source: Additionally, there were no differences in overall activity among all targeted brain regions between groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E; see Figure 3—figure supplement 3 for a brain-wide region activation comparison).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–E

claim: Correlation of neural activity with behavioral performance in each experimental group was weak across all isocortical, hippocampal, and amygdalar subregions analyzed, with the exception of the RSP.
source: Correlation of neural activity with behavioral performance in each experimental group was weak across all isocortical, hippocampal, and amygdalar subregions analyzed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–S), with the exception of the RSP, in which the IS shock group showed strong correlation between eYFP+ cell counts and mean escape latency (r = 0.88, p = 0.02).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–S

claim: In the IS group, the distribution of most significant cortical correlations (p < 0.01) was predominately in motor and somatosensory areas.
source: In both networks, there was a higher proportion of positive correlations in cortical regions. However, the distribution of most significant cortical correlations (p < 0.01) was predominately in motor and somatosensory areas in the IS group, whereas in the CT group, it was biased toward the auditory areas and integrative or associative regions, such as the ectorhinal cortex (ECT).
evidence: Based on analysis of correlation data

claim: In the CT group, the distribution of most significant cortical correlations was biased toward the auditory areas and integrative or associative regions, such as the ectorhinal cortex (ECT).
source: In both networks, there was a higher proportion of positive correlations in cortical regions. However, the distribution of most significant cortical correlations (p < 0.01) was predominately in motor and somatosensory areas in the IS group, whereas in the CT group, it was biased toward the auditory areas and integrative or associative regions, such as the ectorhinal cortex (ECT).
evidence: Based on analysis of correlation data

claim: Both CT and IS networks showed characteristic tailed degree distributions that tend to be found in complex biological systems that follow a power-law distribution.
source: While there was no difference in average degree between groups (Figure 3D), both networks showed characteristic tailed degree distributions that tend to be found in complex biological systems that follow a power-law distribution (Figure 3E; Barabasi and Albert, 1999; Bullmore and Sporns, 2009; Bullmore and Sporns, 2012; Watts and Strogatz, 1998).
evidence: Supported by network analysis data with citations to theoretical work

claim: There was no difference in average clustering coefficient, global efficiency, and mean betweenness centrality between CT and IS networks during LH acquisition.
source: There was also no difference in average clustering coefficient, global efficiency, and mean betweenness centrality (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by network analysis data shown in Figure 3F–H

claim: Trajectories of degree, clustering coefficient, efficiency, and mean betweenness centrality were qualitatively similar between CT and IS groups across a range of alpha thresholds.
source: Trajectories of degree, clustering coefficient, efficiency, and mean betweenness centrality were qualitatively similar between CT and IS groups across a range of alpha thresholds.
evidence: Based on analysis across multiple thresholds

claim: Global topology metrics reveal no striking differences in propensity for information transfer between IS and CT networks during LH acquisition.
source: Thus, global topology metrics reveal no striking differences in propensity for information transfer between IS and CT networks during LH acquisition.
evidence: Based on inference from network analysis results

claim: Many primary somatosensory regions, motor regions, and limbic regions were highly connected in the IS network.
source: The degree distributions revealed that many primary somatosensory (SSp) regions (mouth, SSp-m; lower limb, SSp-Il; barrel field, SSp-bfd; upper limb, SSp-ul), motor regions (primary motor area, MOp), and limbic regions, including the nucleus accumbens (ACB) and BLA, were highly connected in the IS.
evidence: Based on analysis of degree distributions

claim: Far fewer sensory regions showed high degree in the CT networks compared to IS networks.
source: Comparatively, far fewer sensory regions showed such high degree in the CT networks.
evidence: Based on comparison of degree distributions

claim: The AI, PIR, SH, and ENT act as influential information bridges in the IS network.
source: Despite the high connectivity among mostly sensory regions, IS network betweenness distributions showed that additional key structures such as the AI, piriform cortex (PIR), septohippocampal nucleus (SH), and ENT act as influential information bridges in the IS network.
evidence: Based on analysis of betweenness centrality

claim: The AI is a critical region involved in pain processing.
source: The AI is a critical region involved in pain processing (Labrakakis, 2023), and its central network engagement is largely consistent with experiencing a painful sensory event.
evidence: Supported by citation to Labrakakis, 2023

claim: The SUB, ECT, dDG, and MS were most influential in CT networks.
source: In contrast, structures such as the subiculum (SUB), ECT, dorsal dentate gyrus (dDG), and medial septal nucleus (MS) were most influential in CT networks, and betweenness distributions also reveal that the SUB was most influential.
evidence: Based on analysis of betweenness centrality

claim: The subiculum is well known to play a role in spatial representation during exploration.
source: The subiculum is well known to play a role in spatial representation during exploration (Matsumoto et al., 2019; O'Mara et al., 2009), and the MS and dDG are, respectively, involved in motivated locomotion (Mocellin and Mikulovic, 2021) and contextual processing (Tuncdemir et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The MS and dDG are involved in motivated locomotion and contextual processing, respectively.
source: The subiculum is well known to play a role in spatial representation during exploration (Matsumoto et al., 2019; O'Mara et al., 2009), and the MS and dDG are, respectively, involved in motivated locomotion (Mocellin and Mikulovic, 2021) and contextual processing (Tuncdemir et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: The overall patterns seen in the individual regional degree and betweenness distributions indicate a strong engagement of areas involved in contextual and navigational processing in the CT network.
source: The overall patterns seen in the individual regional degree and betweenness distributions indicate a strong engagement of areas involved in contextual and navigational processing in the CT network, whereas there appears to be greater influences of regions involved in sensory and affective processing of shock (e.g., BLA and AI), and motor reactivity (e.g., MOp) in the IS network.
evidence: Based on inference from network analysis results

claim: There appears to be greater influences of regions involved in sensory and affective processing of shock and motor reactivity in the IS network.
source: The overall patterns seen in the individual regional degree and betweenness distributions indicate a strong engagement of areas involved in contextual and navigational processing in the CT network, whereas there appears to be greater influences of regions involved in sensory and affective processing of shock (e.g., BLA and AI), and motor reactivity (e.g., MOp) in the IS network.
evidence: Based on inference from network analysis results

claim: Connections involving either the vCA1, VTA, or PERI were strongly positively correlated in the CT group, whereas they became negatively correlated in the IS group.
source: Specifically, connections involving either the ventral CA1 (vCA1), ventral tegmental area (VTA), or perirhinal cortex (PERI) were strongly positively correlated in the CT group, whereas they became negatively correlated in the IS group (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis data shown in Figure 3L

claim: The VTA is centrally involved in reward processing and functional inversion of its connections may be indicative of the aversive experiencing of inescapable footshocks.
source: The VTA is centrally involved in reward processing and functional inversion of its connections may be indicative of the aversive experiencing of inescapable footshocks.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of VTA function and inference from data

claim: The vCA1 is known to be involved in processing of affective states and fear retrieval, with the vCA1–LHA projection in particular being enriched in representations of anxiety.
source: Additionally, the vCA1 is known to be involved in processing of affective states and fear retrieval, with the vCA1–LHA projection in particular being enriched in representations of anxiety (Jimenez et al., 2018; Jimenez et al., 2020), suggesting functional alterations of this particular connection may be important in the development of LH.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Functional alterations of the vCA1–LHA connection may be important in the development of LH.
source: Additionally, the vCA1 is known to be involved in processing of affective states and fear retrieval, with the vCA1–LHA projection in particular being enriched in representations of anxiety (Jimenez et al., 2018; Jimenez et al., 2020), suggesting functional alterations of this particular connection may be important in the development of LH.
evidence: Based on inference from data and cited literature

claim: The PERI region is involved in object perception and sensory feature processing.
source: Finally, the PERI region is involved in object perception and sensory feature processing (Murray and Richmond, 2001), and thus, its strongly altered connectivity may indicate differences in how sensory features of the environment are assigned an affective value in IS versus CT mice.
